title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
hook: a childless king out hunting hears a baby crying by the river, a small bell at its neck

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa gave Bali his reward: Vishnu at his door, and a flower welcome every Onam. Today the same title turns from Onam to Ayyappa, the god of a forest hill.

A crying sound, thin and high, somewhere near the river. The king of Pandalam is out hunting in the forest, and he stops his horse to listen. It isn't a bird. He follows the sound down to the bank of the Pampa, and there, alone on the ground, is a baby boy, bright as a lamp, with a small bell tied around his neck. No mother. No hut. No one. And the king has no children of his own.
screen: `A CRY BY THE RIVER` → `A BABY WITH A BELL` → `A KING WITH NO CHILDREN`

segments.voice: In the story as it's told in Kerala, a demoness named Mahishi has won a boon that makes her almost impossible to defeat. Only a son born of Shiva and Vishnu together could overcome her, and that sounds like a riddle with no answer. Here's the answer. Vishnu once took the form of Mohini, an enchanting woman, and from Shiva and Mohini a child is born. So Ayyappa is called Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara: Hari is a name of Vishnu, and Hara a name of Shiva. In one small boy, the worship of Shiva and the worship of Vishnu meet. The child is left by the river Pampa with a bell at his neck. The king of Pandalam finds him and longs to keep him. In the telling, a holy man appears and tells the king: take him home, raise him as your son, and the truth will come out in time. So the king carries him back to the palace, and they call him Manikandan, which the story explains as the one with the bell at his throat. The boy who is the son of two gods grows up as an adopted child in a human family, loved by a father who doesn't fully know who he is. Ayyappa's story will soon become a story of a pilgrimage up a forest hill. But it starts with a man who hears a cry and turns his horse toward it.
screen: `MAHISHI'S BOON` · `HARIHARAPUTRA: SON OF HARI AND HARA` · `FOUND BY THE PAMPA RIVER` · `MANIKANDAN, RAISED AS A PRINCE`

segments.voice: Listen for the farthest sound you can hear, then the nearest, then your own breath, letting each one come and go. Then let one face come to mind, someone whose quiet need you might have ridden past this week, and simply turn toward them, the way the king turned his horse. If you pray, you can say the name Ayyappa softly with the breath.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Ayyappa's beginning: the son of Hari and Hara, found as a baby by the Pampa river with a bell at his neck, and raised by the king of Pandalam. Today's word.
Your line: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. A god's story that opens with a foundling and a father who stopped. That's day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Devotees of Ayyappa tell how he was born of Shiva and Vishnu as Mohini, found as a baby by the Pampa river and raised by the king of Pandalam, and the Pandalam royal family keeps a special place in his worship.

notes: The Ayyappa birth and finding story is told in Kerala oral and temple tradition and in later texts (e.g. the Bhutanatha Upakhyanam); the script cites it as Kerala tradition. Keeper: confirm the details and add a textual reference if wanted.
The king of Pandalam is left unnamed (often given as Rajasekhara); confirm.
'Manikandan' explained only as the story explains it ('the one with the bell at his throat'), not as an etymology. Confirm.
The Bhagavata Purana cite is only for Mohini as a form of Vishnu (8.8–8.12, the churning of the ocean); it does not tell the Ayyappa story.
howItsDone mentions the Pandalam royal family's place in Sabarimala worship (e.g. the thiruvabharanam procession) only generally; confirm.
